edition.name: Migne, Patrologia Latina (PL 2, Paris 1844), De virginibus velandis, via Latin Wikisource transcription
edition.witness_note: Single locked witness in repo; second witness not yet locked.

source_text: Sed enim vera, et tota, et pura virginitas nihil magis timet quam semetipsam; etiam foeminarum oculos pati non vult; alios ipsa oculos; habet, confugit ad velamen capitis, quasi ad galeam, quasi ad clypeum, qui bonum suum protegat adversus ictus tentationum, adversus jacula scandalorum, adversus suspiciones, et susurros, et aemulationem, ipsum quoque livorem. Nam est aliquid etiam apud ethnicos metuendum, quod fascinum vocant, infeliciorem laudis et gloriae enormioris eventum. Hoc nos interdum diabolo interpretamur: ipsius est enim, boni odium, interdum Deo deputamus: illius est enim superbiae judicium, extollentis humiles, et deprimentis elatos. Timebit itaque virgo sanctior, vel in nomine fascini, hinc adversarium, inde Deum: illius lividum ingenium, hujus censorium lumen: et gaudebit sibi soli et Deo nota. Sed et si cui innotuerit, sapit si tentationibus gradum obstruxerit. Quis enim audebit oculis suis premere faciem clausam, faciem non sentientem, faciem, ut dixerim, tristem? Quicunque malus cogitatus ipsa severitate frangetur. Jam se etiam mulierem negat, quae virginem celat.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed true and whole and pure virginity fears nothing more than itself; it does not even want to endure the eyes of women; it has other eyes itself; it takes refuge in a veil for its head, as if in a helmet, as if in a shield, which may protect its good against the blows of temptations, against the darts of scandals, against suspicions, and whispers, and envy, and even malice. For there is also something to be feared even among the pagans, which they call fascinum, a more unfortunate outcome of praise and excessive glory. We sometimes interpret this as coming from the devil: for he is the one who hates the good; sometimes we attribute it to God: for He is the one who judges pride, exalting the humble and depressing the proud. The holier virgin will therefore fear, either in the name of fascinum, on the one hand the adversary, on the other God: the former's envious nature, the latter's censorial light; and she will rejoice in being known to herself alone and to God. But even if she becomes known to someone, she is wise if she has blocked the path to temptations. For who will dare to press upon a closed face, a face that does not feel, a face, as I said, sad? Any evil thought will be broken by her very severity. Now she even denies that she is a woman, who conceals that she is a virgin.

choices.why: common Latin term for a type of magical spell or evil eye
refers to God's judging or discerning light

pass_b_english: True, whole, and pure virginity fears nothing more than itself. It refuses to endure even the eyes of other women; it keeps its own eyes for itself. It takes refuge in a head-veil as if it were a helmet, a shield to protect its good against the blows of temptation, the darts of scandal, against suspicions, whispers, envy, and sheer malice. There is even something to fear among the pagans — what they call the *fascinum*, the wretched fallout of praise and outsized glory. We sometimes read this as the devil's work, for he is the hatred of the good; sometimes we ascribe it to God, for he is the judgment on pride, exalting the humble and humbling the proud. The holier virgin will therefore fear, whether you call it *fascinum* or not, both the adversary on one side and God on the other: the one's envious nature, the other's censorial light. She will rejoice in being known to herself alone and to God. Yet even if she becomes known to someone, she acts wisely if she has blocked the path to temptation. Who would dare press his eyes upon a closed face, a face that feels nothing, a face — to put it bluntly — that looks sad? Any evil thought will be shattered by her very severity. She even ceases to count as a woman, the one who hides her virginity.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text. Pass B correctly handles 'ipsa oculos' as 'keeps its own eyes for itself' (or 'it has other eyes itself' in Pass A), and 'deprimentis elatos' as 'humbling the proud'. The final sentence 'Jam se etiam mulierem negat, quae virginem celat' is correctly rendered in both versions, capturing the paradoxical sense that by concealing her virginity (via the veil), she denies her status as a mere woman.
